text: Solana rent is a one-time, fully refundable minimum-balance deposit, not a recurring fee. An account must hold (128 + data_len) x lamports_per_byte lamports. The 128 is fixed storage overhead. text: The JLP-market price impact fee has two parts. text: When account keys are passed, Agave returns for each slot the larger of the block minimum and the highest minimum fee recorded for any of those writable accounts (a std::cmp::max over per-account minimums). An account's minimum is kept only if it exceeds the block minimum, and only writable accounts are tracked. Agave's own struct comment calls this 'the minimum fee needed to land a transaction'. Chainstack draws the practical consequence: each returned value is a floor, so an average or median of the values is an average or median floor, not the fee actually paid. text: Solana prices contention per writable account, not network-wide. Transactions compete when they write the same account, so a hot account raises fees only for transactions that touch it. Agave's cache records minimum fees per writable account. Helius docs say 'Solana prices priority fees per writable account'. RPC Fast and OrbitFlare tell builders to estimate from the accounts their transaction writes, not from network-wide medians. text: Handle retries on the client. Rebroadcast the same signed bytes every couple of seconds until the transaction confirms or its blockhash expires, and track lastValidBlockHeight (Triton: the transaction can land up to lastValidBlockHeight + 1). Do not re-sign with a new blockhash until getBlockHeight is above that value and getSignatureStatuses shows the original absent, because both signed versions can execute. Treat a transaction as landed at confirmed or finalized, since a processed transaction can be dropped on a minority fork. Triton says maxRetries has no effect on its endpoints. QuickNode and Chainstack suggest maxRetries 0 with your own rebroadcast loop. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

text: Raydium separates price impact from slippage and tolerance. Price impact, impact = (p_before - p_after) / p_before, is a deterministic property of a trade against a specific pool state and can be computed before submission (about 2 x amount_in / reserve_in for small constant-product trades; piecewise on CLMM pools). Realized slippage is (quoted_out - actual_out) / quoted_out. Tolerance is a buffer around the impact: minAmountOut = amountOut x (1 - tolerance), so a 2% impact with 0.5% tolerance puts the floor about 2.5% below pre-trade spot. (low confidence)

text: Triton's getRecentPrioritizationFees accepts a 'percentile' integer from 1 to 10,000 (5000 = median; 0.01% to 100.00%). Values above 10,000 are rejected, and omitting it returns the standard minimum. For each of up to 150 recent blocks it returns the percentile of compute-unit prices paid by non-vote transactions. With account addresses it takes that percentile over the transactions that write-lock each account and returns the highest of those values. The client still has to aggregate the per-slot values. The example client makes two parallel calls, with and without percentile, so it falls back to the standard result on other providers. The method is a Triton extension that needs a validator patch (tag v1.17.23-getrpf of rpcpool/solana-public), and the example repo calls it 'currently in beta testing'. text: Only the program that owns an account can debit it, so excess rent on a program-owned account (PDA) stays until that program ships a reclaim instruction. A safe instruction verifies the account's owner and the authority's signature, reads the floor from Rent::get() at call time, moves only the excess, and credits exactly what it debits. System Program wallets have no separate excess to reclaim. (high confidence)

text: Revival attack: a program that closes an account by zeroing its lamports does not delete it until the transaction ends. An attacker adds a transfer in the same transaction that refunds the rent, and the account survives. Safe closing moves the lamports, reassigns the owner to the System Program and shrinks the data. Current Anchor close() does this: it credits the destination, sets lamports to 0, calls assign(system_program::ID) and resize(0), and rejects closing an account into itself. (high confidence)

text: SIMD-0392 (Activated; authors Igor Durovic and Jon C of Anza) lets an existing account stay below the current rent-exempt minimum if its pre-execution balance is above zero, its size does not grow and its owner does not change. The floor is then min(current minimum, pre-execution balance). Growth or an owner change requires the current minimum. Chainstack dates its mainnet activation at slot 443,664,000. This grandfathering makes a later rate increase non-disruptive. (high confidence)

text: SPL Token CloseAccount deletes a token account and sends all its lamports (rent plus any extra) to a destination chosen by the owner or the close authority, who signs. It fails with InvalidAccountData if source and destination are the same account, and with NonNativeHasBalance if a non-native account still holds tokens. A frozen account with a zero balance can still close. The account that paid to create an associated token account gets nothing back automatically. (high confidence)

text: Only the owning program can debit a program-owned account, so excess rent on a program's PDAs needs an instruction in that program. The Foundation's checklist: verify the account is owned by the program, verify the authority signer, read the floor from the Rent sysvar, move only the excess, and conserve lamports across the transaction. Programs you do not control often have no such instruction. (high confidence)

text: A rent sponsor that pre-funds accounts can lose the deposit. Turnkey's rent sponsorship (an Enterprise-plan feature, off by default) pre-funds the signer for new accounts, and the refund goes to the close destination, usually the signer or owner, not the sponsor. Turnkey's mitigations: strip CloseAccount (discriminator 9) before submission, set Jupiter's wrapAndUnwrapSol to false and manage wrapped SOL explicitly, reuse a constrained set of token accounts, and apply deny policies, spend caps and monitoring. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)
